planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in dappled shade after the last hard frost, siting where the deep crimson spring bells and fiery fall foliage can be seen up close.

directions: This botanical variety, originally collected on the island of Shikoku, is prized for flower clusters that are noticeably darker and more uniformly crimson-red than the species, with the same nodding, bell-shaped, cream-veined-red form. Grow in acidic, evenly moist, well-drained woodland soil high in organic matter, and avoid alkaline sites where chlorosis will develop. Site in light shade or morning sun with afternoon protection to preserve flower color and prevent leaf scorch. Prune only lightly right after flowering to shape, since next year's buds set on the current season's growth; established plants need little supplemental water beyond a summer mulch layer.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Nymans Skimmia (Heavy-Berrying Female Evergreen Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant a male Skimmia pollinator such as 'Rubella' or 'Kew Green' within about 15 feet to guarantee the heavy, long-lasting red berry set this cultivar is grown for.

directions: Selected at the Nymans garden in Sussex, this female clone is valued for producing an especially dense, long-persisting crop of bright red berries against dark, glossy evergreen foliage from fall well into winter. It needs a nearby male Skimmia to pollinate its small, fragrant, creamy-white spring flower clusters. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic to neutral soil in full to partial shade, since strong sun and dry soil both cause yellowing and leaf scorch. Mulch annually to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity, and avoid heavy pruning, as flower and fruit buds form on the previous year's wood.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

common_name: Wakehurst White Skimmia (White-Berried Dwarf Evergreen Shade Shrub)

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained shade beds or containers; this self-fertile dwarf form needs no separate pollinator to set its ivory-white berries.

directions: Named for a selection made at Wakehurst Place, this compact, self-fertile form of the reevesiana subspecies bears clusters of unusual porcelain-white berries in autumn rather than the typical red, contrasting nicely with its dark, leathery evergreen leaves. Because it is self-fruitful, a single specimen produces fruit without a separate male plant nearby. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; unlike the straight species, this subspecies tolerates slightly more alkaline conditions but still performs best where soil stays consistently moist. Its low, mounding habit suits shaded foundation plantings, woodland edges, and shady containers, and it needs only minimal shaping after flowering.

common_name: Robert Fortune Skimmia (Compact Heavy-Fruiting Female Evergreen)

planting.note: Site near a male Skimmia pollinator in acidic woodland soil for the heaviest berry display from this compact female selection.

directions: Named in honor of the plant collector who introduced Skimmia japonica to Western gardens, this female cultivar forms a tidy, rounded mound of glossy evergreen foliage and produces an unusually heavy crop of bright scarlet berries when a male pollinator is planted nearby. Its more compact stature than many female Skimmia selections makes it well suited to small shade borders, mixed woodland plantings, and foundation beds. Grow in cool, humus-rich, acidic to neutral soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, in dappled to full shade. Refresh mulch yearly to hold moisture and soil acidity, and limit pruning to light shaping right after the spring bloom.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich soil in a sheltered, partly shaded site so the very early spring flower racemes escape late frost damage.

directions: Native to central China, this winter hazel species produces long, pendulous racemes of soft primrose-yellow, faintly fragrant flowers on bare branches in very early spring, distinguished from other Corylopsis by its notably broad, rounded floral bracts. Grow in acidic to neutral, well-drained soil enriched with leaf mold or compost, in a site sheltered from strong wind and late-season frost, which can damage the precocious blooms. Partial shade with some morning sun brings out the best flowering and clean yellow-green summer foliage; deep, occasional watering during dry spells keeps the shallow root system from stressing. Prune only to remove damaged wood immediately after flowering, since next year's buds form on the current season's growth.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
